constellation/antlia.description: Antlia (the Air Pump) is a faint southern constellation created by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in the 18th century to honour the air pump invented by Robert Boyle.

constellation/aquila.description: Aquila the Eagle is a constellation on the celestial equator, containing the bright star Altair at its centre.

constellation/bootes.description: Boötes the Herdsman is a constellation containing Arcturus, the fourth brightest star in the night sky.

constellation/capricornus.fun_fact: Capricornus is one of the oldest recognised constellations, appearing in Babylonian star catalogues over 3,000 years ago!

constellation/cepheus.fun_fact: Cepheid variables discovered by Henrietta Leavitt revolutionised astronomy by allowing us to measure cosmic distances!

constellation/chamaeleon.description: Chamaeleon is a small southern constellation introduced by Dutch navigators in the late 16th century, representing the colour-changing lizard.

constellation/hercules.fun_fact: Our solar system is moving towards a point in Hercules called the solar apex at about 20 km/s!

constellation/horologium.description: Horologium (the Pendulum Clock) was created by Lacaille to honour Christiaan Huygens' invention of the pendulum clock in 1656.

constellation/mensa.description: Mensa (Table Mountain) was created by Lacaille to honour Table Mountain in Cape Town, South Africa, where he made his observations of the southern sky.

constellation/microscopium.description: Microscopium (the Microscope) was created by Lacaille to honour the compound microscope. It's one of the faintest constellations in the sky.
constellation/microscopium.fun_fact: Microscopium's brightest star, Gamma Microscopii, was once part of neighbouring Sagittarius — it was reassigned when constellation boundaries were standardised in 1930!

constellation/octans.description: Octans (the Octant) was created by Lacaille to honour the navigational instrument. It contains the south celestial pole.

constellation/orion.description: Orion the Hunter is one of the most recognisable constellations, visible from both hemispheres with its distinctive Belt of three stars.

constellation/puppis.fun_fact: Puppis contains M47, an open cluster visible to the naked eye that was "lost" for over 200 years due to a cataloguing error!

constellation/sagittarius.description: Sagittarius the Archer points towards the centre of our Milky Way galaxy, making it rich in nebulae and star clusters.
constellation/sagittarius.fun_fact: When you look at Sagittarius, you're looking toward Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at our galaxy's centre!

constellation/scutum.description: Scutum (the Shield) was created by Hevelius in 1684 to honour King John III Sobieski of Poland. It is one of the few constellations named for a non-mythological historical figure.

constellation/telescopium.description: Telescopium (the Telescope) was created by Lacaille to honour the invention of the refracting telescope. It lies south of Sagittarius and Corona Australis.

constellation/ursa_major.description: Ursa Major (the Great Bear) contains the Big Dipper asterism, one of the most recognised star patterns in the northern sky.

dso/blue_snowball_nebula.description: The Blue Snowball is a planetary nebula in Andromeda — the glowing shell of gas expelled by a dying star. At magnitude 8.3 it is one of the brightest and most colourful planetaries in the sky, appearing as a vivid blue-green disk even in small telescopes. Its symmetrical shape and intense colour make it a favourite amongst observers.

dso/lmc.description: The Large Magellanic Cloud is an irregular satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, visible to the naked eye as a detached, glowing patch of sky. It is one of our closest galactic neighbours and one of the most active star-forming galaxies in the Local Group.

dso/m104.fun_fact: The Sombrero Galaxy has a supermassive black hole at its centre estimated to be 1 billion solar masses!

dso/m110.description: M110 is a dwarf elliptical galaxy and satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy, the last object added to the Messier catalogue.
dso/m110.fun_fact: M110 was actually observed by Messier in 1773 but not added to his catalogue until 1966!

dso/m13.fun_fact: In 1974, the Arecibo message was beamed towards M13 as an attempt to contact extraterrestrial intelligence!

dso/m14.fun_fact: In 1938, a nova appeared in M14 but wasn't discovered until 1964 when old photographic plates were examined!

dso/m2.fun_fact: M2 contains about 150,000 stars and has a diameter of 175 light-years, making it one of the largest globular clusters!

dso/m22.description: M22 is one of the nearest and brightest globular clusters to Earth, located in Sagittarius near the galactic centre.

dso/m39.fun_fact: At around 825 light-years, M39 is one of the nearest open clusters to Earth, and at roughly 240 million years old it is one of the older naked-eye clusters — old enough that its most massive stars have already ended their lives. Messier recorded it in 1764 and it was amongst the earliest additions to his catalogue.

dso/m40.description: M40 is unique in the Messier catalogue — it is not a nebula, cluster, or galaxy, but a wide double star. Messier catalogued it in 1764 whilst searching for a nebula reported by Johann Hevelius in Ursa Major, found only this pair of stars, and recorded it so that future observers would not mistake it for something more interesting.

dso/m43.description: De Mairan's Nebula is a detached portion of the great Orion Nebula complex, separated from M42 by a dark dust lane but belonging to the same vast molecular cloud. Named after French astronomer Jean-Jacques Dortous de Mairan, who noted it in 1731, it is an emission nebula ionised by the hot young star NU Orionis embedded at its centre.

dso/m45.fun_fact: The Pleiades are amongst the nearest star clusters to Earth and have been recognised by virtually every ancient civilisation!

dso/m51.fun_fact: The Whirlpool was the first galaxy to be recognised as having spiral structure, discovered by Lord Rosse in 1845!

dso/m53.fun_fact: M53 is one of the most distant globular clusters from the galactic centre at 60,000 light-years away from it!

dso/m66.fun_fact: M66's asymmetric appearance is caused by gravitational interactions with its neighbours M65 and NGC 3628!

dso/m77.fun_fact: M77 harbours an active galactic nucleus with a black hole 15 million times the mass of our Sun!

dso/m78.fun_fact: M78 contains about 45 young T Tauri variable stars, very young stars still contracting towards the main sequence!

dso/m81.fun_fact: M81 is gravitationally interacting with neighbouring galaxy M82, triggering intense star formation in M82!

dso/m82.fun_fact: M82 is forming stars 10 times faster than our Milky Way due to gravitational interaction with neighbouring M81!

dso/m9.description: M9 is a compact globular cluster in Ophiuchus — one of the Messier globulars most affected by interstellar dust absorption. It lies towards the galactic bulge, where thick dust dims it significantly. Without this obscuration M9 would appear nearly a magnitude brighter and be visible to the naked eye.

dso/willman_1.fun_fact: For every unit of ordinary matter in Willman 1, there are roughly 660 units of dark matter — making it amongst the most dark-matter-dominated objects ever discovered. Its stars also show signs of tidal disruption as the Milky Way slowly pulls it apart.

moon/europa.description: Europa is the second Galilean moon and is thought to harbour a vast liquid water ocean beneath its icy crust, making it one of the most promising places to search for life.

moon/io.fun_fact: Io has hundreds of active volcanoes, some erupting lava fountains dozens of kilometres high. Its constant activity is driven by tidal heating from Jupiter's enormous gravity.

moon/phobos.fun_fact: Phobos orbits Mars so quickly it rises in the west and sets in the east — and it is slowly spiralling inward, destined to either crash into Mars or break apart into a ring in about 50 million years.

planet/sun.description: The Sun is the star at the centre of our solar system. It provides the light and heat that makes life on Earth possible.
planet/sun.fun_fact: The Sun contains 99.86% of all the mass in our solar system. About 1.3 million Earths could fit inside it!

shower/aquariids.description: The Eta Aquariids are one of two annual showers produced by debris from Halley's Comet. Peaking at up to 70 meteors per hour, the shower strongly favours the southern hemisphere, where the radiant rises high before dawn. Northern observers still enjoy a respectable rate of 30 or more per hour.
shower/aquariids.fun_fact: Eta Aquariid meteors travel at 66 km/s — fast enough that the ionised air they create can glow for several seconds after the meteor has gone. You may see Halley's ancient dust burning up in front of your eyes, shed during one of the comet's many visits thousands of years ago.

star/alcyone.fun_fact: Alcyone is actually a multiple star system with at least three companions! It also spins so fast that it has a disc of gas around its equator.

star/alkaid.fun_fact: Unlike most stars in The Plough, Alkaid is not part of the Ursa Major Moving Group — it's travelling through space in a different direction, so The Plough's shape will slowly change over thousands of years!

star/antares.description: Antares is a red supergiant star, the heart of Scorpius (the Scorpion). Its name means "rival of Mars" due to its red colour.

star/arcturus.fun_fact: Arcturus is travelling through space at a tremendous speed and will pass closest to our solar system in about 4,000 years!

star/fomalhaut.fun_fact: Fomalhaut has a spectacular debris disc that was one of the first to be directly imaged around another star!

star/izar.fun_fact: The 19th-century astronomer Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve called Izar "Pulcherrima" (Latin for "most beautiful") because of the stunning colour contrast between its orange and blue-white components!

star/kaus_australis.fun_fact: Kaus Australis lies near the direction of the centre of our Milky Way galaxy! When you look at this star, you're gazing toward the densest part of the galactic plane.

star/markab.description: Markab is one of the four stars forming the Great Square of Pegasus, an easily recognisable asterism.

star/menkar.fun_fact: Menkar is nearing the end of its stellar life. This ageing red giant is fusing helium in its core and will eventually shed its outer layers to become a planetary nebula!

star/procyon.description: Procyon is a bright star in the constellation Canis Minor (the Lesser Dog). It's one of our closer stellar neighbours.

star/scheat.description: Scheat is a red giant star in the Great Square of Pegasus, notable for its deep orange-red colour.
